column1: What is the fundamental contract of the block device abstraction?
column2: Storage is exposed as a one-dimensional array of fixed-size blocks, each addressed by a logical block address (LBA), with constant-time read/write access—hiding seek latency, erase-before-write constraints, and physical media complexity.

column1: Why did the industry transition from 512-byte to 4096-byte (4 KiB) physical sectors?
column2: Larger sectors reduced per-sector format overhead and improved error correction efficiency as storage density increased.

column1: What is the core engineering tradeoff in choosing filesystem block size?
column2: Smaller blocks reduce internal fragmentation for small files but increase metadata overhead; larger blocks improve sequential throughput but waste space on small files.

column1: What foundational invariant did the inode design establish in Unix-like filesystems?
column2: File identity is bound to the inode number, not to the pathname—filenames are merely directory entries mapping strings to inode numbers.

column1: What happens to an inode's data when all hard links are removed but a process still has the file open?
column2: The data blocks are NOT reclaimed; the in-memory open file descriptor reference keeps the inode alive even though it's invisible to directory listings. Only on final close() does the kernel release storage.

column1: Why is renaming a file within the same filesystem an O(1) operation regardless of file size?
column2: Rename only modifies a directory entry (the name-to-inode mapping); it does not touch the inode or any data blocks.

column1: What is the space efficiency formula for a bitmap-based block allocator tracking N blocks?
column2: N/8 bytes, since each block requires exactly one bit (0 = free, 1 = allocated).

column1: Compare bitmap vs. free-list block allocation tradeoffs.
column2: Bitmaps are space-efficient (N/8 bytes) but require sequential scanning to find contiguous free regions. Free-lists enable O(1) allocation but incur metadata overhead and fragment over time.

column1: What indexing structure does the canonical Unix inode use to map logical file offsets to physical blocks?
column2: A multi-level indexing tree: direct blocks (inline pointers) for small files, with indirect/double-indirect/triple-indirect blocks for larger files requiring additional indirection levels.

column1: Define the crash consistency invariant that filesystems must preserve.
column2: After any crash, the filesystem must reflect either the state immediately before a sequence of operations began, or the state immediately after all operations completed—never a partial intermediate state.

column1: What is the distinction between logical consistency and data consistency in crash recovery?
column2: Logical consistency ensures metadata structures satisfy internal invariants (e.g., every allocated block referenced by exactly one inode). Data consistency ensures user data is fully written or not written at all, avoiding torn writes.

column1: What discipline do journaling filesystems impose to solve the crash consistency problem?
column2: Write-ahead logging: filesystem structure changes are recorded in a journal before the actual metadata structures are modified in place, enabling fast replay-based recovery instead of full fsck scans.
